newsitem.title: USA: NY Pataki vows federal welfare bonus to go for aid.
newsitem.headline: NY Pataki vows federal welfare bonus to go for aid.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki, who failed to get the Assembly to approve welfare reforms he proposed last spring, on Wednesday released a new plan and vowed that a $450 million bonus would be used for public aid.
New York has to approve a new welfare plan to comply with the dramatic federal reforms that were signed into law in August.

Pataki's latest program fleshes out a preliminary outline that the Republican governor last month sent to Washington for its approval, so that it would fully qualify for a new block grant of as much as $2.36 billion.

The state's $450 million federal bonus will be split, with $105 million going to the state, $105 million to local governments, and the balance "put in the system in one way or another," Pataki said. He added $150 million would be used as a cushion to help deal with local governments and providers.
Pataki's new program, which contains a number of the same provisions that the Assembly rejected, includes a plan to gradually cut cash benefits until they end after five years.

But slashing the benefits will not save the state or local governments any money. "The phase out of the benefits, which would not take place for the first 18 months, all of those savings will be reinvested in the system in the form of job training, day care and other support services," he said.

A total of $630 million, an increase of $130 million, would be spent on childcare, employment and other support services, with more than $700 million, a $70-million rise, spent on employment services. And people who work while on welfare will be able to keep up to $1,080 a month, up from $667 a month, without having their benefits cut.

Saying that his Administration has cut welfare rolls by almost 220,000, more than any other state, Pataki focused heavily on the workfare aspects of the new plan, which will be called "NY Works." The state already has placed more than 50,000 participants in work activities, so it only needs to find slots for another 17,000, he said.

Pataki confidently predicted that the state, which has added 120,000 private sector jobs in the past two years, will continue to grow employment. However, the workfare parts of program were among the first that were questioned by the state comptroller and advocacy groups.
New York State faces an especially difficult task in grappling with the new federal welfare reforms because Article 17 of the state constitution obliges it to care for the needy.

Pataki's new plan calls for ending the state-funded Home Relief program, which aids able-bodied single adults and childless couples. It will be replaced with a "Saftey Net" that will replace cash benefits will be replaced with vouchers, food, shelter and medical assistance.

The Safety Net, which also will help people who have reached the end of the five-year limit on welfare benefits, also aims to satisfy the state's constitutional obligation to care for the needy and cover emergencies for the destitute.

Asked if the Safety Net plan would satisfy the consitutional requirement, Pataki said "There's no question it shouldn't. I'm not one to predict what the courts may or may not do, but the constitution is very clear that the safety net is as determined by the legislature and the governor, and that is what we will be doing under this program."
Pataki promised to lobby Washington to soften some of the federal rules, like ones cutting benefits for legal immigrants who arrive after federal law was enacted on August 22.
